questions.stem: A 75-year-old man was admitted from his nursing home with several days of fever, nonproductive cough, headache, and diarrhea. The nursing staff mentioned that two other patients had also been unwell and had had fevers and respiratory symptoms. On admission, the patient had a temperature of 38.5°C, pulse of 110 beats/minute, blood pressure 98/50 mmHg, and oxygen saturation of 89% on room air. His initial laboratory evaluation was notable for a sodium of 125, creatinine of 1.6, and white blood cell count of 16,000. Chest radiograph showed bilateral, diffuse, interstitial, pulmonary opacities. Cultures were ordered, and broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy was initiated.
questions.lead_in: Of the listed antibacterials, which of the following would be most likely to be effective against the causative pathogen?
questions.explanation: Azithromycin This patient is presenting with a syndrome compatible with atypical pneumonia. It is also noteworthy that there was a cluster of sick patients at his nursing home, which could be suggestive of a spreading respiratory viral infection or Legionella, which has been associated with hospital and nursing home-related outbreaks because of contaminated water sources. Hyponatremia, acute renal failure, abnormal liver function tests, and gastrointestinal symptoms may be seen with legionellosis. Other causes of atypical pneumonia can include M. pneumonia and C. pneumonia, which can also be treated with azithromycin.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q37

parts.text: Name 2 organisms that can be transmitted by aerosols, but are not thought to be transmitted person-to-person.

questions.question: 12 year old patient with Crohns on TNF alpha who came back from vacation with family in august with 3 days history of fever, non productive cough and diarrhea. Admitted for respiratory distress with CXR of multilobar pneumonia. Started on piptazo. Worsened and requires admission to PICU with hypoxemic respiratory failure.

parts.text: What is the likely syndrome
Name 2 investigations with one advantage and disadvantage each (table: Test / Advantage / Disadvantage)
Name 2 antimicrobial classes that can be used to treat this infection and two drugs within that class that are first line (table: Antimicrobial class / Drug 1 / Drug 2)

questions.model_answer:
a) Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumophila pneumonia) - suggested by severe multilobar community-acquired pneumonia with diarrhea, failure to respond to beta-lactam therapy (piperacillin-tazobactam), and a host with TNF-alpha inhibitor-related immunosuppression (a recognized risk factor for Legionella).
b) Table - Test / Advantage / Disadvantage:
Urinary antigen test / Rapid, simple to perform, requires no special expertise, remains positive for weeks after infection (useful even after antibiotics started) / Only reliably detects Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 - insensitive (<5-60%) for other serogroups and non-pneumophila species.
Sputum/respiratory culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar / Most specific test, allows species/serogroup identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and permits matching to environmental (e.g., water system) isolates for outbreak investigation / Slow (several days to result), technically demanding, requires specialized media/expertise not available in many laboratories, and lower sensitivity than antigen/PCR testing.
c) Table - Antimicrobial class / Drug 1 / Drug 2:
Macrolide / Azithromycin / Clarithromycin.
Fluoroquinolone / Levofloxacin / Moxifloxacin.

questions.question: Multifocal pneumonia in ICU not responding to Tazobactam and has hepatitis and hyponatremia (Na 127).

parts.text: What is the organism
What are 2 diagnostic tests and 1 advantage and disadvantage of each
What are 3 agents to treat it

questions.model_answer:
a) Legionella pneumophila (Legionnaires' disease) - suggested by lack of response to piperacillin-tazobactam, multifocal pneumonia, transaminitis, and hyponatremia (Na 127), all classic features of LD.
b) Table - Test / Advantage / Disadvantage:
Urinary antigen test / Rapid, simple to perform, requires no special expertise, remains positive for weeks after infection (useful even after antibiotics started) / Only reliably detects Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 - insensitive (<5-60%) for other serogroups and non-pneumophila species.
Sputum/respiratory culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar / Most specific test, allows species/serogroup identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and permits matching to environmental (e.g., water system) isolates for outbreak investigation / Slow (several days to result), technically demanding, requires specialized media/expertise not available in many laboratories, and lower sensitivity than antigen/PCR testing.
c) Three treatment agents: azithromycin, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin (doxycycline is an alternative if macrolides/fluoroquinolones cannot be used).

questions.question: Two patients in your hospital have acquired Legionella pneumonia. The source is suspected to be the potable water distribution system in your hospital.

parts.text: What are TWO short-term solutions that can be implemented to immediately reduce the risk of infection?
What are THREE long-term solutions to prevent the risk of infection in the future?

questions.model_answer:
a) Two short-term solutions to immediately reduce risk from a contaminated potable water system: (1) Superheat-and-flush of the hot water system (raise water temperature to ≥70°C/158°F and flush all outlets/taps). (2) Hyperchlorination of the water system, and/or temporary installation of point-of-use filters on faucets and showerheads in high-risk patient care areas.
b) Three long-term solutions: (1) Implementation of a formal water management program (e.g., per ASHRAE 188) with regular risk assessment and monitoring for Legionella. (2) Installation of a supplemental disinfection system, such as copper-silver ionization or chlorine dioxide/monochloramine treatment of the water supply. (3) Engineering modifications to the plumbing system (e.g., eliminating dead legs/areas of water stagnation, optimizing hot water temperature control) to reduce ongoing colonization risk.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC/ASHRAE 188 water management program guidance for healthcare facility Legionella control.

questions.question: A patient on a TNF-alpha inhibitor is admitted to the hospital. They have a rapid pneumonia. They are placed on PTZ, but are not improving. Blood work given and Na low at 127.

parts.text: What is the diagnosis?
What are 2 tests you can do and a limitation of the testing.
What are 2 drug treatment classes.
What is 1 alternative drug you could use?

cohort_answer.text: Legionella pneumophila. TNF-alpha inhibitors increase risk of intracellular pathogens (2-4 fold increase in TB and other granulomatous conditions; also Listeria, Legionella, Salmonella, HBV, VZV, JC virus, possible NTM/Nocardia, case reports of Crypto/Histo/Cocci). Tests: Urine legionella antigen (only detects serogroup 1) and culture (needs specialized charcoal-containing media); can also do DFA. Treatment classes: fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin), macrolides (azithromycin). Alternative: doxycycline.

questions.question: Legionella outbreak. You suspect your hospital potable water system.

parts.text: Name 2 short term interventions you can implement now (1)
Name 3 long term interventions you can implement to prevent Legionella overgrowth in the water system (1.5)

cohort_answer.text: Short term: Immediately stop using potable water linked to the site causing the outbreak; Immediately treat water system as per local policy. Long term: Scheduled water testing; Scheduled water treatments; Ensure IPC involved in all future construction/renovations so that interventions are in place to avoid future outbreaks

parts.text: 2 causes of infectious dermatitis from hot tub exposure?
1 (or 2) causes of pneumonia from hot tub exposure
Most common parasitic cause of widespread waterborne diarrheal illness?

cohort_answer.text: Dermatitis: Hot tub folliculitis (Pseudomonas aeruginosa) - painful pruritic pustules within 24-48h, self-resolves 7-14d; Hot foot syndrome (Pseudomonas) - painful red nodular lesions on soles, self-limiting 7-10d; Green nail syndrome (pseudomonas) with onychomycosis; Mycobacterium species. Pneumonia: MAC hypersensitivity pneumonitis ('hot tub lung'), usually self-limiting, may need prednisone +/- antimycobacterial; Legionellosis (usually L. pneumophila). Parasite: Giardia lamblia (most common cause of parasitic diarrhea worldwide; cryptosporidium also very high incidence); tx metronidazole/tinidazole/nitazoxanide, paromomycin if pregnant first trimester
